description:
I'm Ben, a software developer, and this will be my fourth time participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. I bring experience in software development, technical leadership, process automation, and software engineering.

Team Enterprise was inspired by the spaceship that symbolizes exploration, courage, and innovation.
summary:
Earth Jukebox turns real NASA Earth observations into music, so people can perceive change on our planet by listening, not only by looking. It is built for the general public and for blind or low-vision users who can't read a traditional chart.
Eleven experiences use data from NASA EONET, GIBS and the Earth Information Center (SVS visualizations): Hurricane Helene, the Hunga Tonga eruption, night lights, lightning seen from the ISS, atmospheric carbon, forest height, aerosols, sea temperature and currents, air quality and an atmospheric river. One rule applies to all of them: intensity picks the note and chord, and speed of change picks the tempo.

Whoever learns it in one phenomenon can hear the others.
Measurements are taken in the browser at run time, for example the Tonga plume pixel by pixel in GOES-West infrared frames, and the lit area of the planet in annual night-light frames. Each phenomenon plays with a Brazilian accent (baião, maracatu, samba, bossa nova) or a universal synth accent. It has a 3D globe, spatial audio, voice narration, phone vibration, full keyboard operation and PT/EN/ES. Models, estimates and illustrations are labeled as such. Only real NASA data is used.
details:
What it does: Earth Jukebox maps NASA data to sound. Wind speed, pressure, plume area, pixel brightness and color, and position (latitude picks the pitch, longitude picks the stereo side) become notes, chords, tempo and 3D panning. Instruments enter when a measurement crosses a scientific threshold, such as the Saffir-Simpson categories.

How it works: Hurricane Helene's track and intensity come from the EONET API, and satellite imagery comes from GIBS (NOAA-20, Aqua, Terra, GOES-West, Black Marble), which also provides the Hunga Tonga frames. Nine more experiences use frames from NASA SVS visualizations on the Earth Information Center, processed by one shared engine. A sweep line reads one measure per pixel column and plays a bell for each. Three.js draws the real-globe 3D scene. Tone.js and the Web Audio API synthesize the sounds that follow the data (chords, melody, bells, textures); an optional recorded background track (made with Suno) can play underneath and follows the tempo of the data. There is no backend for the data. A small serverless function only proxies voice narration. A ?local mode runs from saved copies of the real NASA responses, so the demo works with poor internet.

About data: The night-light, CO2, forest and lightning experiences use visualization frames, not calibrated radiance, so they compare one year with another and show what is in view, not a world value. CO2 and aerosols are model outputs. Lightning in the Helene and Tonga scenes is illustrative. The labels in the interface say so.

Accessibility: The product works without sight: audio, voice narration, vibration, keyboard-only use, and VLibras (Brazilian Sign Language) support. We have not tested it with blind users.
dataRefs: NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker)
NASA SVS - Change in Night Lights 2012-2023 (SVS 5313)
NASA SVS - Lightning seen from the ISS (SVS 5011)
